## The Last Morning

At 4:17 every morning, the service elevator in the Hill Street Apartments stopped between the eighth and ninth floors, though the building had only eight. Junie had worked the night desk for twenty-three years and knew every fault of the machine: the warm shudder, the sigh of the belts, the way the doors held open one heartbeat longer than necessary. But she had never seen a ninth-floor button appear.

That morning, it glowed like a tiny moon.

A man in a rain-dark coat stood inside. He carried a cup of tea and a ring of keys.

“Good,” he said, as if they had an appointment. “You’re new.”

“I work on eight.”

“You’ll work on nine now.”

The button had no number. When Junie pressed it, the elevator rose without any sensation of movement. The man siped his tea. Rain ticked against the windows, though the sky had been clear when she arrived.

On the ninth floor, a long corridor waited. It smelled of dust, oranges, and distant grass. Every door was labeled with a date.

“This is where the city keeps its mornings,” the man said.

Junie thought he was making a joke. He unlocked the first door.

Beyond it was a circular room lined with shelves. Thousands of glass jars stood on the shelves, each containing a small, luminous sky. Some shone blue and gold. Others were gray, rose-colored, or the deep violet of late evening. In one jar, rain fell endlessly over an empty street. In another, sunlight moved slowly across the stones of a river.

Junie leaned closer. A tiny figure ran through one of the mornings, arms spread, chasing a dog whose legs seemed made of lightning.

“Is that a person?”

“Once,” said the man. “Or nearly.”

He explained that people often lost parts of their days. Not hours—those were accounted for—but mornings. The moment before waking. The first sip of coffee. The unexpected song from an upstairs window. A face across a crowded room. These things entered the world so gently that, without someone to notice them, they fell through the hours and gathered here.

“We give them away,” he said. “Every morning should belong to someone.”

Junie looked at the jars. There were far too many.

“Who takes them?”

“People do. They come upstairs with a question, and we open a jar. Sometimes they discover what they lost. Sometimes they decide they never had it.”

The man placed a ninth-floor key in her palm.

“My name is Alister. I am retiring.”

“Retiring where?”

“Outside.” He gestured toward the windows. The rain was falling upward now, returning to the clouds. “The position is yours, if you want it.”

Junie closed her fingers around the key. It was warm from someone else’s hand.

“Why me?”

“Because you have a morning you’d like back.”

Before she could answer, every jar in the room began to tremble.

Alister glanced at the ceiling. One of its beams had split.

“The building can hold only so many,” he said. “Before you take over, you must dispose of one jar.”

“Destroy it?”

“Release it.”

He led her to a worktable in the center of the room. A brass funnel rested above a silver basin.

“Choose a morning,” he said, “and let it return.”

Junie read the labels for a long time. She considered a beach at sunrise, when she and her mother had walked barefoot along the shore. She considered Christmas Eve, when her daughter had fallen asleep on her lap while carols drifted from the radio. She considered so many mornings that choosing felt like betrayal.

At last, she selected an ordinary Tuesday in October, six years old.

The label read: *8:02. Rain. Toast with too much butter. The word “mama,” spoken once from a bed, unnoticed.*

Junie remembered.

Her daughter, small and sleep-tousled, had stood in the kitchen doorway holding a blue cup. Junie had been reading the newspaper. She had answered without looking up: “What?”

The girl had asked for more milk.

There had been no great speech, no lesson in love. Only a child asking for milk and a mother too distracted to turn the page.

Junie opened the jar.

The morning smelled of rain and warm toast. For a moment, nothing happened. Then the light in the jar climbed over her hands, crossed her wrists, and spilled into the room.

Every other jar began to glow.

Alister took her arm. “Come. This is more than one morning.”

They stepped outside as the ceiling cracked. Across the city, windows brightened in waves. People stirred beneath their blankets. A bakery worker turned on a radio and heard the first birds of spring. A man on a night bus looked up and remembered his wife laughing. Somewhere near the river, two people who had passed each other in the dark stopped and reached for one another’s hands.

The rain stopped.

Junie watched the clouds break apart. Sunlight entered the streets in narrow golden bars. Somewhere in the city, her daughter opened her eyes.

That evening, the telephone rang.

“Hello?” Junie said.

For a moment, there was only breathing.

Then her daughter said, “I woke up remembering something.”

“What?”

“I don’t know. There was a cup. Blue, maybe. I was standing in the kitchen, and I was asking for something. I think I asked for you.”

Junie pressed her hand against her mouth.

“I was there,” she said. “I think I was distracted.”

“You always were.”

There was a pause, but it was not unkind.

“I remember telling you that I was sorry,” her daughter continued. “Maybe I didn’t say it then. Maybe I’ve said it enough now.”

“Yes,” Junie said. “More than enough.”

After they hung up, she returned to the ninth floor. The shelves were empty, the windows clear. Dawn spilled across the floorboards.

Alister stood beside the brass funnel.

“Every keeper is allowed one morning,” he said. “Not for looking back. For beginning.”

Junie took a fresh jar from the cupboard.

She placed it beneath the funnel. Above her, the first morning of the new day leaned close to listen.

And Junie, who had spent so long noticing everything except the life directly before her, began to pay attention.
